segments.title: The fleet gap behind the Gorshkov class
segments.body: The retirement of Krivak frigates and Sovremenny destroyers left a gap in Russia's surface fleet. The Udaloys were being kept going as the newest destroyers still available. Some traditional destroyer duties therefore passed to frigates, including the visible presence missions that had been a major part of the destroyers' work. The Gorshkov class needed both military capability and enough presence to advertise Russia's navy abroad.

evidence.note: Krivak and Sovremenny retirements, efforts to retain the Udaloys, and the transfer of destroyer presence duties to frigates.

segments.summary: Russia needed a frigate that could take on some of the work of its Soviet-era destroyers.

segments.title: The Soviet shipbuilding inheritance
segments.body: Soviet institutions built the shipyards and infrastructure that Russia inherited. They also trained generations of workers whose experience continued to shape shipbuilding after the Soviet Union ended. A change of state did not erase decades of accumulated knowledge. The Gorshkov class combines that industrial inheritance with the Russian Navy's demand for capability and a visible international presence.

evidence.note: Soviet-built yards and infrastructure, generations of training, and the persistence of that experience in a frigate intended for capability and presence.

segments.summary: The class inherited Soviet shipyards, infrastructure and generations of shipbuilding experience.

segments.title: How launcher capacity changed within Project 22350
segments.body: The baseline Project 22350 fit is given as 48 vertical launch system (VLS) cells: 16 roughly strike-length cells and 32 tactical-length cells. The upgraded ships receive 32 of each, for a total of 64. In those figures, all the additional capacity comes from the longer-cell bank. The length labels are approximate descriptions of the two groups. These fits belong to the original Gorshkov series and should be distinguished from the larger Project 22350M proposals considered later.

evidence.note: Baseline 16 plus 32 cells and upgraded 32 plus 32 cells, using roughly strike-length and tactical-length labels before the explanation of opportunities to upgrade.

segments.summary: The stated upgrade doubles the longer-cell bank from 16 to 32 while retaining 32 shorter cells, raising the total from 48 to 64.

segments.title: How the loss of a turbine supplier slowed construction
segments.body: Design studies began in the 1990s, approval followed in 2003 and the first ship was laid down in 2006. War with Russia's gas turbine supplier then disrupted an already lengthy programme. A ship's power and operating systems are designed around its turbines, so replacing the supplier entails substantial redesign. Domestic production introduces another delay because the manufacturing capability has to be established.

evidence.note: Design studies in the 1990s, permission in 2003 and first keel in 2006, followed by turbine supply disruption requiring redesign and domestic manufacturing capacity.

segments.summary: Project 22350 shows how losing a supplier can delay an entire ship when the propulsion system was designed around its equipment.

segments.title: Gorshkov construction, fitting out and commissioning
segments.body: The Gorshkov programme combines modern-looking ships with design work dating to the 1990s. The figures quoted are ten planned and five complete, although two of those five are still fitting out and only three are counted as in service. Completion therefore does not consistently mean operational entry in these figures. One ship's status is disputed, with January 2027 suggested as a possible date for full commissioning. That date remains a forecast, and the uncertainty prevents treating the totals as a settled fleet inventory.

evidence.note: Ten planned, five called complete including two still fitting out, three in service, and a disputed status with commissioning tentatively expected in January 2027.

segments.summary: The programme figures distinguish three ships in service from two still fitting out, despite describing all five as complete.

segments.title: Why a single shipyard complicates tracking individual frigates
segments.body: Severnaya Verf in Saint Petersburg builds the ships while several hulls are at different stages of construction. Information about work at the yard can be difficult to assign to a particular vessel. Parts attributed to one build may belong to several, complicating estimates of individual progress. Publicly released information supports the broad claim that construction is continuing, while verification of each hull's status remains uneven.

evidence.note: Different construction stages at Severnaya Verf, difficulty assigning parts to individual builds, and reliance on public information for the broad construction claim.

segments.summary: Construction at Severnaya Verf makes it difficult to establish which components belong to which Gorshkov hull.

segments.title: The 3S14 launcher family and the production pause
segments.body: The longer 3S14 cells offer a choice of Oniks, Kalibr or Zircon missiles. An upgraded launcher, 3S14M, is associated with Project 22350M. The distinction between that proposed derivative and upgraded ships of the original series remains unclear at this point. A production pause forced by missing equipment also gives designers time to revise the ship's systems. Equipment upgrades can therefore accompany the eventual resumption of construction.

evidence.note: Oniks, Kalibr and Zircon options for 3S14, a 3S14M association with 22350M, and the opportunity to upgrade during a supply-driven pause. The boundary between upgraded original ships and the proposed derivative is unclear.

segments.summary: The 3S14 missile options illustrate the frigate's flexibility, while a forced pause in construction creates an opportunity to upgrade equipment.

segments.title: The S-350 family and the frigate's air defence
segments.body: The frigate's air defence is linked to the S-350 family. Reported performance in conflicts is the basis for judging the system credible, without treating it as an exceptional new development. A 2019 service-entry date accompanies the explanation that much of the underlying work is older. The date is not clearly assigned to the shipboard installation. The same ambiguity limits how directly the family's reported performance can be applied to the frigate.

evidence.note: Naval air-defence link to S-350, a qualified positive judgement based on reported conflict performance, and a 2019 service date whose application to the shipboard installation is unclear.

segments.summary: The S-350 lineage supports a judgement that the frigate's air defence deserves respect, though the family's reported performance is not clearly separated from that of the naval installation.

segments.title: The post-Soviet gap in engineering and training
segments.body: The Soviet breakup brought economic disruption that affected Russia's skilled workforce. Gaps developed among experienced engineers and other key personnel. Training schools and the routes that supplied new staff also suffered disruption, making replacement of those skills difficult. These disruptions made it harder to sustain the engineering workforce behind weapons development.

evidence.note: Post-Soviet economic problems, shortages of experienced engineers and key personnel, and disruption to training schools and recruitment pipelines.

segments.summary: Economic upheaval and disrupted training left Russia with gaps in experienced engineers and other personnel needed for weapons development.

segments.title: Cold War studies and the S-350's later development
segments.body: The S-350's development lineage reaches back to studies near the end of the Cold War. Formal work is dated to 1999, separating the earlier studies from the later programme. Possible information acquired from South Korea and elsewhere is mentioned tentatively. No specific contribution or transfer arrangement is identified, so that suggestion cannot establish how much foreign work influenced the system.

evidence.note: Late Cold War studies, official work beginning in 1999, and tentative reference to information acquired from South Korea and other places without details of its contribution.

segments.summary: The S-350's origins are traced to late Cold War studies, with formal work dated to 1999 and possible South Korean input left uncertain.

segments.title: Why threat assessment must take an opponent's weapons seriously
segments.body: Personal attitudes towards a country do not determine the effectiveness of its weapons. The recommended planning assumption is that an opponent's systems work and deserve respect. Planning around supposed incompetence creates a dangerous surprise if the equipment proves effective. Arrogance in assessing a threat can cost lives.

evidence.note: National likes and dislikes are a poor basis for judging weapons, with an explicit recommendation to assume effective systems and a warning about casualties from arrogance.

segments.summary: Assuming that an opponent's weapons are ineffective because of national prejudice can lead to operational surprise and casualties.

segments.title: Air-defence missile range, speed and manoeuvrability
segments.body: The upper range quoted for the air-defence missiles is 120 km, with range varying by missile type. High speed and manoeuvrability are also credited to the weapons. Those characteristics underpin the judgement that the frigate's air defence deserves respect. No particular missile variant is identified for the 120 km figure.

evidence.note: Range up to 120 km across different missile types, high speed and high manoeuvrability, without a specific variant tied to the range claim.

segments.summary: A quoted range of up to 120 km, together with high speed and manoeuvrability, underpins the positive assessment of the air-defence missiles.

segments.title: Anti-ship reach and the limits of an improvised range estimate
segments.body: The anti-ship missile estimate begins with roughly 800,000 square nautical miles of coverage. An improvised calculation then puts the range near 900 miles before revising it to about 895. The area and linear-distance figures are not reconciled, and the distance's unit is less specific than the area's. They should therefore be treated as an uncertain spoken estimate of reach. The qualitative conclusion is that the frigate's anti-ship weapons pose a threat that other forces must take into account.

evidence.note: Approximately 800,000 square nautical miles of anti-ship coverage followed by mental arithmetic revising roughly 900 miles to 895. The area-to-distance relationship and distance unit remain unresolved.

segments.summary: The anti-ship coverage estimate shifts between area and distance, leaving the numerical range uncertain while stressing the frigate's offensive reach.

segments.title: The Gorshkov class's anti-submarine equipment
segments.body: The Gorshkov class can carry a helicopter and has sonar for anti-submarine work. Those capabilities support a judgement that the frigate has credible anti-submarine capability alongside its missile roles. The evaluation remains general: no helicopter or sonar model is named, and no detection performance is specified.

evidence.note: Helicopter carriage and sonar support a positive but general judgement of anti-submarine capability, without equipment models or performance figures.

segments.summary: The frigate's helicopter and sonar give it an anti-submarine role alongside its missile armament.

segments.title: A larger Project 22350M and a possible S-400 adaptation
segments.body: The largest proposed launcher fit reaches 128 cells, divided into 64 longer cells and 64 shorter cells. A possible naval adaptation of the S-400 would probably occupy some of the larger cells. Further changes to those cells are also considered possible, so simply increasing the total would not settle compatibility. Both the launcher arrangement and the S-400 installation remain prospective features.

evidence.note: Potential 64 plus 64 launcher arrangement and possible naval S-400 adaptation, with larger-cell use and additional cell modifications explicitly speculative.

segments.summary: A possible 128-cell derivative raises the question of whether a naval S-400 adaptation would need larger or further-modified launch cells.

segments.title: When the enlarged Gorshkov looks like a destroyer
segments.body: The 128-cell proposal puts the enlarged Gorshkov firmly in the destroyer category in this judgement. The concern extends to how other navies would treat the ship. Its armament would make it a destroyer-like target even if it retained the frigate label. Classification here concerns the ship's military importance and exposure to enemy attention, without establishing a universal cell-count threshold for destroyers.

evidence.note: A 128-cell ship is judged a destroyer and expected to attract a destroyer's targeting attention, even under a frigate designation.

segments.summary: A 128-cell Gorshkov would attract the attention and targeting priority of a destroyer, whatever its official designation.

segments.title: Launcher placement and the 130 mm gun in the enlarged design
segments.body: The proposed ship's launcher layout could retain separate groups of similar cells or mix the cell types more widely. Another choice is between concentrating all the launchers forward and placing some aft. A prediction based on Russian design preferences favours a more dispersed arrangement with launchers aft. More gun armament is also considered possible. The 130 mm gun is judged a solid weapon that Russia values, supporting the expectation that it would be retained. These are design predictions, with the final layout still unsettled.

evidence.note: Homogeneous or mixed launcher groups, all-forward or fore-and-aft placement, a prediction of dispersed cells, and possible retention or expansion of the valued 130 mm gun armament.

segments.summary: The enlarged design leaves open whether to mix launcher types, distribute cells fore and aft, or increase the 130 mm gun armament.

segments.title: Neustrashimyy and the case for a first serial stealth frigate class
segments.body: The Neustrashimyy frigates already had stealth features before the Gorshkov class. Their widely spaced construction supports an interpretation of them as technological test beds as much as operational frigates. The case for calling Gorshkov Russia's first real stealth frigate class rests on bringing such capabilities into repeat production. That is a judgement about the pattern of construction, with the earlier ships' signature-reduction features explicitly acknowledged.

evidence.note: Earlier Neustrashimyy stealth features and widely separated builds underpin a test-bed interpretation and the claim for Gorshkov as the first real production class.

segments.summary: The earlier Neustrashimyy frigates had stealth features. The case for giving the Gorshkov class a first rests on repeat production.

segments.title: Port visits and Russian naval diplomacy
segments.body: Port visits put a country's navy in front of a foreign audience and can carry soft-power value. The Gorshkov frigates have made those visits and conducted visible presence missions for Russia. Pyotr Velikiy and Admiral Kuznetsov attracted more attention, with concern about a breakdown adding to the carrier's publicity. The frigates' visits are credited with attracting favourable attention and providing useful diplomatic presence.

evidence.note: Soft-power value of port visits, Gorshkov presence missions and favourable attention, compared with the greater publicity around Pyotr Velikiy and breakdown concerns surrounding Kuznetsov.

segments.summary: The frigates' port visits show how a smaller warship can project presence and draw attention abroad.

segments.title: The competing Project 22350M proposals
segments.body: The upgraded Gorshkov earns a stronger endorsement than the original version, while Project 22350M or Super Gorshkov remains a further proposal. One option has 48 cells of each type, for 96 in total. Another combines 64 strike cells with 32 anti-aircraft cells, reaching the same total with a different balance. The 96-cell option is still entertained as a frigate, while the maximum 128-cell version is firmly judged a destroyer. These alternatives leave both the final configuration and the laying-down date unresolved.

evidence.note: Positive judgement of upgraded Gorshkov, alternative 48 plus 48 and 64 strike plus 32 anti-aircraft fits for the proposed derivative, and a 128-cell maximum judged a destroyer with no settled laying-down date.

segments.summary: Two proposed 96-cell fits divide the weapons differently, while the largest Super Gorshkov option reaches 128 cells. The construction timetable remains uncertain.
